title: Clozapine Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Famous trade names: Clozaril and Leponex
It is atypical antipsychotic medication (new, second generation) and the first atypical to be discovered
It is mainly used in treatment of schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder in resistant cases
Clozapine was synthesized in 1958 by the Swiss pharmaceutical company Wander AG
Pharmacokinetics
Available as oral formula only
It is well absorbed with bioavailability of 60% due to first pass metabolism
Metabolized extensively by the liver via CYP enzymes, especially CYP1A2 and excreted through urine and feces
Elimination half life is 14 hours
Mechanism of action
clozapine antagonizes serotonin 5HT receptors and dopamine receptors
Serotonin antagonism makes clozapine good in managing the negative symptoms of schizophrenia, like social isolation, poverty of speech, lack of motivation and inability to feel pleasure
Antagonism of serotonin by this medication also lead to relief of some of the extrapyramidal side effects that occur as a result of dopamine antagonism
BUT serotonin antagonism lead to weight gain and metabolic changes as adverse effects with the use of this medication
Clozapine antagonizes dopamine but it has higher affinity to dopamine D4 receptors more than D2 receptors which lead to less extrapyramidal symptoms compared to other antipsychotics
Dopamine antagonism in the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathway which lead to relieving of the positive symptoms of schizophrenia
It also blocks dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway but it has lower risk of hyperprolactinemia compared with other antipsychotics
It has anti histamine activity which lead to drowsiness
It also block muscarinic receptors including M1, 2, 3, 5; it is agonist at M4
It blocks alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree too
Therapeutic uses

Use of clozapine in treatment of schizophrenia has shown better symptoms control and reduced risk of hospitalization and drug discontinuation but it is not used as a first line because it may lead to agranulocytosis and GIT hypomotility which may kill the patient (that will be discussed in the adverse effects part of this article)
It is used in treatment of schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder in:
Patients who didn’t have adequate response to two other antipsychotic medications (resistant cases)
Patients who are unable to tolerate other antipsychotics due to extrapyramidal side effects
Patients who develop tardive dyskinesia while on some other antipsychotic medication
It is used in treatment of psychosis that occur as a side effect to Parkinson’s disease treatment
It is used for reducing risk of suicide in people with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder who has high suicide risk
Third line in treatment of manic phase of bipolar disorder (lithium being first line, other atypicals being second line)
According to FDA, max dose is 900 mg/day, average dose is 300 mg/day for women and 400 mg/day for men

Clozapine used as a second line because it may lead to agranulocytosis (agranulocytosis likely to be fatal) in the first year and a half of treatment, after that risk reduces, also because it lead to GIT hypomotility (surprisingly most common cause of death from this medication more than agranulocytosis even)
clozapine lead to bone marrow suppression and agranulocytosis (1% of cases) which is severe neutropenia less than 500 /mm
Risk factors for agranulocytosis are old age, female, concurrent tx with medications that cause same condition, monitor with CBC
It may lead to GIT hypomotility which may lead to severe constipation, fecal impaction, paralytic ileus, bowel obstruction, acute megacolon, ischemia or necrosis
It may lead to myocarditis (3% of cases) which is inflammation of the heart muscle, also fatal
Risk factors for myocarditis include rapid titration of the drug, concurrent use of SSRIs, illicit substance abuse
Most common adverse effect of clozapine is hypersalivation in 60% of the patients, clozapine is agonist in M4 which is highly expressed in salivary glands
Weight gain, high blood sugar levels due to serotonin antagonism
It also block alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree leading to postural hypotension and palpitation
Increased risk of death if used in patient with dementia related psychosis
Extrapyramidal symptoms are not common with this medication because of its anticholinergic effects and serotonin antagonism and its higher affinity for dopamine D4 more than D2 receptors
Increase risk of seizures in seizure disorders patients
Anticholinergic side effects: Elevated temperature, sedation, constipation and urinary retention
Periorbital edema (rare)
Clozapine withdrawal
Abrupt withdrawal of clozapine lead to cholinergic rebound effects, those include
Drug interactions
Fluvoxamine (SSRI), theophylline, ciprofloxacin all inhibit metabolism of the medication leading to increased blood levels and overdose
Carbamazepine increase metabolism of this medication leading to low plasma levels and treatment failure and it also increase risk of agranulocytosis
Clozapine overdose
Symptoms of overdose include sedation, confusion, tachycardia, seizures and ataxia

title: Risperidone Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Famous trade name is Risperdal
It is atypical antipsychotic medication (new, second generation)
It is used in treatment of schizophrenia and some other mental disorders and it is better tolerated than typical antipsychotics because of fewer side effects
Risperidone synthesized in 1980 in Belgium
Pharmacokinetics
Risperidone is available as oral, IM, and IV formulas, there is long acting injectables with duration of action of 2-4 weeks
Long acting formulas provide improved compliance and reduced relapse rates compared to oral formulas
Oral formula of the risperidone has good absorption with bioavailability of 70%
It is metabolized by the liver by CYP enzymes especially CYP2D6
Excreted mainly through urine and it also excreted through feces
Mechanism of Action
Risperidone antagonizes serotonin 5HT receptors and dopamine D2 receptors
BUT it has more serotonin antagonism than dopamine antagonism and that what it make different from typical antipsychotics
Serotonin antagonism makes risperidone good in managing the negative symptoms of schizophrenia, like social isolation, poverty of speech, lack of motivation and inability to feel pleasure
Antagonism of serotonin by this medication also lead to relief of some of the extrapyramidal side effects that occur as a result of dopamine antagonism
BUT serotonin antagonism lead to weight gain and metabolic changes as adverse effects with the use of this medication
Risperidone work by antagonizing dopamine D2 receptors in the brain
It blocks dopamine in the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathway which lead to relieving of the psychosis
It also blocks dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway which lead to extrapyramidal symptoms as adverse effects
It also blocks dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway lead to hyperprolactinemia as an adverse effect
It has anti histamine activity which lead to drowsiness
It blocks alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree too
FDA Approved Therapeutic Uses
Schizophrenia (in adults and children aged 13 and older): risperidone is more effective in treating schizophrenia than all typical antipsychotics except for haloperidol
Acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar disorder: as monotherapy for adults and children aged 10 and older
Acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar disorder: as adjunctive with lithium or valproate
Autism in children aged 5 and older: risperidone controls problematic behaviors, aggression, self injury and rapid mood changes
Non FDA Approved Therapeutic Uses
Dementia: they produce slight benefits in dementia patients, but there is increase risk of death (because it increase risk of stroke)
Psychotic polydipsia
PTSD, delirium, depression, borderline personality, conduct disorder and Tourette disorder

For schizophrenia: start with 1 mg daily then increase the dose by 0.5 mg every six to seven days to target 2 mg daily, doses exceeding 4 mg per day are rarely more effective, max dose is 16 mg per day; for elderly same dose except you increase by 0.25 mg every six to seven days instead of 0.5 mg
For acute manic episodes of bipolar disorder: 2 to 3 mg daily dose, max dose is 6 mg per day
Daily dose in both disorders can be taken at once or divided into two doses
Weight gain, high blood sugar levels and metabolic problems
Hyperprolactinemia lead to sexual dysfunction
Increase risk of seizures in seizure disorders patients
Extrapyramidal symptoms (movement disorders): risperidone produce more extrapyramidal symptoms than other atypical antipsychotics does
Acute dystonia: muscle spasm develops within hours to days after initiation
Akathisia: restlessness develops days to months after initiation
Tardive dyskinesia: uncontrollable repetitive movements develops after years of initiation
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Autonomic disturbance
There is increased risk of death if haloperidol is used in elderly patient with dementia related psychosis, that is why it is not FDA approved for this use
Contraindications
Previous hypersensitivity reaction to the risperidone or paliperidone (risperidone metabolite)

title: Haloperidol Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Famous trade name is Haldol
It is classified as high potency typical antipsychotic drug from butyrophenones family
Used in treatment of schizophrenia and some other mental disorders
Haloperidol was discovered in 1958 by the Belgian physician Paul Janssen
Pharmacokinetics
Available as oral, IM and IV formulas
Good absorption of oral formula with bioavailability of 60-70%
Distribution: haloperidol is heavily protein bound by 90%, free part distributed to different body tissues
Metabolized by the liver through glucuronidation and CYP oxidation by CYP3A4
Excreted through bile and urine
Mechanism of action
Haloperidol work by antagonizing dopamine D2 receptors in the brain
It blocks dopamine in the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathway which lead to relieving the psychotic symptoms
It also blocks dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway which lead to extrapyramidal symptoms as adverse effects
It also blocks dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway lead to hyperprolactinemia as an adverse effect
Haloperidol also has anti serotonin, antimuscarinic and anti histamine activity
It blocks alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree too
Therapeutic uses
Psychotic disorders like schizophrenia and acute psychosis
Tics in Tourette syndrome
Manic phase of bipolar disorder
Agitation and aggressive behavior
Alcohol withdrawal
Treatment of intractable hiccups
Severe nausea and vomiting not responding to first line medications
For schizophrenia and Tourette syndrome: dose is 0.5 to 2 mg orally 2 to 3 times a day, max dose is 30 mg/day
For acute agitation: 2 to 5 mg intramuscular every 4 to 8 hours
Treatment considerations
In long term use of haloperidol for schizophrenia and other chronic disorders, daily dose should be reduced to the lowest level possible for maintenance
In long term use of this medication, routine monitoring including measurement of BMI, BP, fasting blood sugar, and lipid profile is recommended due to risk of side effects
Extrapyramidal symptoms (movement disorders): those are more common than with use of other antipsychotics
Acute dystonia: muscle spasm develops within hours to days after initiation
Akathisia: restlessness develops days to months after initiation
Tardive dyskinesia: uncontrollable repetitive movements develops after years of initiation
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Autonomic disturbance
Anticholinergic side effects: elevated temperature, dry mouth, sedation, constipation and urinary retention
Hyperprolactinemia which lead to erectile dysfunction in males, amenorrhea, galactorrhea in females
It also block alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree leading to postural hypotension, reflex tachycardia and palpitation
Eye Lens opacities if haloperidol used for long time , because it accumulates in the lens
QT interval prolongation => torsades de pointes
Contraindications
Previous hypersensitivity reaction in the individual
Parkinson’s disease
Lewy body dementia
CNS depression, coma patients, concurrent use with barbiturates, benzodiazepines and opioids
There is increased risk of death if haloperidol is used in elderly patient with dementia related psychosis, that is why it is not FDA approved for this use
IV use with higher doses may lead to torsades de pointes arrhythmia and sudden death
Motor instability, orthostatic hypotension may lead to falls and fractures while on this medication
Haloperidol toxicity
Symptoms of toxicity include
Severe extrapyramidal symptoms
Coma with severe respiratory depression
There is no antidote for Haloperidol and treatment is supportive
Gastric lavage and activated charcoal
ABCs, endotracheal intubation and ventilation
IV fluids, albumin and vasopressors
Drug Interactions
Amiodarone: both prolong QT interval => torsades de points
Amphetamine and methylphnidate: haloperidol antagonize the action of norepinephrine and dopamine in patients taking these medications
Epinephrine: haloperidol antagonize eipinephrine leading to decrease BP
Levodopa: antagonize
Lithium: rare cases of encephalopathy if these medications used together
Methyldopa: increased extrapyramidal side effects

CYP inducers and inhibitors affect metabolism of haloperidol: inducers such as carbamazepine , phenobarbital and rifampicin associated with low levels of haloperidol, inhibitors such as quinidine, buspirone and fluoxetine associated with higher plasma levels of haloperidol
Tricyclic antidepressant metabolism decreases if used with haloperidol together and this might lead to toxicity

title: Chlorpromazine Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Famous trade names: Thorazine and Largactil
Classified as low potency typical antipsychotic drug from phenothiazines family
Used in treatment of schizophrenia and some other mental disorders
Chlorpromazine was developed in 1950 and it was the first antipsychotic
Pharmacokinetics
Chlorpromazine is available as oral, IM, IV formulas
Oral absorption is variable with bioavailability of 10-90%
Widely distributed through the body, high lipid solubility so it easily crosses blood brain barrier to CNS
Extensively metabolized in the liver by CYP enzymes especially CYPA12 and 2D6, also metabolized by kidney and GIT
Excreted in urine
Mechanism of Action
Chlorpromazine works by antagonizing dopamine D2 receptors in the brain
Blocks dopamine in the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathway → relieves psychotic symptoms
Blocks dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway → extrapyramidal symptoms as adverse effects
Blocks dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway → hyperprolactinemia as an adverse effect
Also has anti-serotonin, antimuscarinic, and anti-histamine activity
Blocks alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree too
Therapeutic Uses
Treatment of psychosis including schizophrenia
Manic phase of Bipolar disorder
Treatment of chronic hiccups
Treatment of nausea and vomiting not responding to first line medications (anti-emetic effect from blocking dopamine, histamine, and muscarinic receptors in vomiting center)
Treatment of agitation and severe anxiety
Off label: migraine and serotonin syndrome
For schizophrenia
Oral: start 25-75 mg/day orally twice per day, maintain at 200 mg/day, max 800 mg/day
IM/IV: 25 mg then 50 mg after 1-4 hours, repeat, dose can be 300-800 mg/day
For nausea and vomiting
Oral: 10-25 mg every 4-6 hours as needed
IM/IV: 25-50 mg every 4-6 hours as needed
Extrapyramidal symptoms (movement disorders): tremor, dyskinesia, akathisia (less than other typicals)
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
More anticholinergic side effects (blurred vision, dry mouth, sedation, constipation)
Blocks alpha adrenergic receptors → postural hypotension
Mild bone marrow suppression
Increased prolactin → decreased libido, gynecomastia, galactorrhea, erectile dysfunction
Contraindications
Previous hypersensitivity reaction to the drug
CNS depression, coma
Bone marrow suppression
Hepatic failure and acute liver disease
Pheochromocytoma
Risk of closed angle glaucoma in elderly patients taking this medication

title: Antipsychotic Drugs Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Antipsychotics also known as Neuroleptics.
Drugs that block the dopamine receptors in the central nervous system.
They used in treatment of psychosis and schizophrenia.
To understand antipsychotics, first we need to understand psychosis and schizophrenia and how they happen.
Psychosis is a set of symptoms that occurs due to many medical and psychiatric disorders like schizophrenia, psychotic depression, delirium.
Psychosis is characterized by loss in the perception of reality in the affected person (living in a type of dream).
Psychosis symptoms include:
Delusions: false unshakable beliefs (could be persecutory or grandiose)
Hallucinations: false perception of external stimuli (could be auditory, visual, gustatory, smelling..)
Disorganized thought: content and form of thoughts
Schizophrenia is a mental disorder, characterized by recurrent episodes of psychosis, cognitive dysfunction and negative symptoms.
Schizophrenia is associated with positive symptoms (psychotic symptoms): delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thought and abnormal behavior.
Schizophrenia associated with cognitive impairment in form of difficulty processing information, decreased attention and troubles with memory.
It is also associated with negative symptoms in form of poverty of speech, social isolation, lack of motivation and inability to feel pleasure.
Schizophrenia symptoms are caused by increase dopamine levels in some dopaminergic pathways.
Now, let’s explain the dopaminergic pathways and how they are affected by schizophrenia and antipsychotics.
Dopaminergic Pathways
There is 4 major dopamine pathways in the brain, they include:
Mesolimbic pathway
Mesocortical pathway
Nigrostriatal pathway
Tuberoinfundibular pathway
Mesolimbic Pathway
Transmit dopamine from ventral tegmental area in the midbrain to the ventral striatum (formed by nucleus accumbens and olfactory bulb).
Mesolimbic pathway functions related to reward cognition (wanting response, pleasure response from certain stimuli) and aversion cognition (strong dislike).
Increasing dopamine levels in the mesolimbic pathway lead to psychosis and schizophrenia.
Antipsychotics block dopamine in this pathway to control psychotic symptoms.
Mesocortical Pathway
Mesocortical pathway transmits dopamine from the ventral tegmental area to the frontal cortex.
Mesocortical pathways related to executive functions.
Increasing the dopamine levels in the mesocortical pathway lead to schizophrenia.
Antipsychotics block dopamine in this pathway to control psychotic symptoms.
Nigrostriatal Pathway
Nigrostriatal pathway transmits dopamine from substantia nigra to the caudate nucleus and putamen (all these are parts of the basal ganglia).
Nigrostriatal pathway related to motor functions, reward related cognition and associative learning.
Decreasing the levels of dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway leads to extrapyramidal side effects similar to Parkinson’s disease.
Parkinson’s is a movement disorder characterized by tremors, dyskinesia, cogwheel rigidity, stooped posture and shuffling gait (explained more in adverse effects chapter of this video).
When antipsychotics blocks dopamine, it also block it in this pathway leading to Parkinson’s like symptoms.
Tuberoinfundibular Pathway
Transmits dopamine from hypothalamus to the pituitary gland.
This pathway function is to regulate prolactin secretion.
If dopamine levels decrease in this pathway, this lead to hyperprolactinemia.
Antipsychotics block dopamine in this pathway, thus leading to hyperprolactinemia.
This lead to side effects like decrease libido, sexual dysfunction, infertility.
Classification of Antipsychotics
Typical antipsychotics (AKA old antipsychotics, first gen antipsychotics), developed in 1950s Chlorpromazine
Atypical antipsychotics (AKA new antipsychotics, second gen antipsychotics), developed in 1970s Risperidone
Clozapine (used in resistant cases)
Mechanism of Action of Typical Antipsychotics
They block a lot of receptors, mainly dopamine D2 receptors.
That is why they are more likely to be associated with extrapyramidal symptoms like tremors and dyskinesia.
Mechanism of Action of Atypical Antipsychotics
They block the dopamine D2 receptors but to lesser degree than typicals do, they also block the serotonin 5HT receptors, muscarinic and alpha adrenergic receptors.
They are associated with lower incidence of extrapyramidal symptoms that typical antipsychotics.
With the use of atypicals, there is high risk of metabolic adverse effects, such as weight gain, hypercholesterolemia and DM.
Therapeutic Uses

Both typicals and atypicals are used in schizophrenia, atypicals are used as the first line nowadays because they produce less extrapyramidal symptoms, but typicals has much better efficacy that atypicals in managing schizophrenia positive symptoms.
Cases where there is no sufficient response to typicals and atypicals (refractory cases) then clozapine is used (watch for bone marrow suppression).
Negative symptoms of schizophrenia are better managed with the atypicals.
Chlorpromazine sometimes used to relieve intractable hiccups.
Typicals are used in treatment of severe nausea and vomiting because they block dopamine D2 receptors in chemoreceptor trigger zone in medulla.
Antipsychotics also used in treatment of agitation and aggressive behavior secondary to other disorders (e.g. autism).
Pimozide (typical antipsychotic) is indicated for treatment of tics in Tourette disorder.
Antipsychotics also used in management of manic and mixed episodes of bipolar disorder.
Paliperidone (atypical) used in treatment of schizoaffective disorder.
Antipsychotics also used in treatment of depression refractory to antidepressants and other treatment lines.
Extrapyramidal manifestation: those occur as a result of blocking Dopamine D2 receptors in nigrostriatal pathway (in the basal ganglia), they include: Tremor: shaking movements
Rigidity (hypertonia): resistance to passive movement
Dystonia: sustained muscle contractions, usually occurs within few hours to days of the treatment
Akathisia: inability to remain still
Rigidity and tremor occur within weeks to months after starting treatment
Dyskinesia: involuntary repetitive muscle movement, that occur with long term treatment with antipsychotics
The extrapyramidal manifestations can be treated by administration of anticholinergic drug that work on CNS (benztropine)
Akathisia respond better to beta blockers (e.g. propranolol)

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: Serious complication with mortality rate of 20%. Occur with typical antipsychotics. Present as autonomic disturbance in form of muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, high blood pressure, sweating and myoglobinemia. Treatment with stopping of the antipsychotic and supportive.
Hyperprolactinemia occur more with typical antipsychotics, and it lead to sexual dysfunction, gynecomastia and amenorrhea
Antipsychotics blocks alpha receptors leading to postural hypotension and light headedness, this occur especially with atypical antipsychotics
Some antipsychotics block muscarinic receptors (chlorpromazine, clozapine and olanzapine) leading to anticholinergic effects like blurred vision, dry mouth, confusion and constipation
Weight gain, hyperglycemia more with atypical antipsychotics because of 5HT receptor blockage
Clozapine lead to agranulocytosis
Cardiac arrhythmias with chlorpromazine
Cholestatic jaundice
Antipsychotics may increase seizures in seizure disorders patients
They carry increased mortality if used in elderly patients with dementia and psychosis
They may lead to suicidal ideation or behaviors if used in mood disorders patients

title: Novalgin Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Classification of analgesics
Opioid analgesics
Analgesics antipyretics drugs: e.g. paracetamol, Novalgine and nefopam
Non analgesic drugs that work as analgesics for some conditions: e.g. carbamazepine (antiepileptic drug) used for trigeminal neuralgia, duloxetine (anti depressant) used for diabetic neuropathy
Scientific name is metamizole or dipyrone, trade name is Novalgin
it is an analgesic, antispasmodic and antipyretic medication
It was first synthesized in 1922 in Germany
Novalgin is banned in some countries due to studies suggesting severe drug adverse effects such as agranulocytosis
Pharmacokinetics
It is available in oral, IM and IV formulations
Oral formula is well absorbed with 100% bioavailability
Metabolized by liver and excreted in urine and feces
Elimination half life is 14 minutes for parent compound and 2-4 hours for its metabolites (active metabolites)
Mechanism of action
MOA is unknown, theory: it work by inhibiting brain and spinal cord prostaglandins to relieve pain and fever, it also work as antispasmodic
Therapeutic uses
It is used as analgesic for moderate to severe pain, e.g. peri and post operative pain, colic, cancer pain and trauma related pain
it has more potent analgesia than aspirin but it has no anti inflammatory action
Agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia (bone marrow suppression)
Compared to NSAIDS, Novalgin causes less kidney, CVS and GIT side effects
It may trigger bronchospasm or anaphylaxis (especially in asthma)
It also trigger another hypersensitivity reactions like toxic epidermal necrolysis because it is chemically related to sulfonamides
Contraindications
Previous hypersensitivity reactions to the same drug or to sulfonamides
Impaired hematopoiesis (e.g. during chemotherapy)
Third trimester of pregnancy and lactation
Children with body weight less than 16 kg

title: Nefopam (Acupan): Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Scientific name is Nefopam, trade name is Acupan
Non opioid, centrally acting analgesic medication
It was originally synthesized in 1960
Pharmacokinetics
Available in oral and IV formulations
Oral formula is well absorbed with low bioavailability
After absorption it is bound by 70% to plasma proteins are the rest is distributed to the tissues, especially brain where it exert its effects
Metabolized by the liver and excreted through urine and bile
Elimination half life is 3 to 8 hours
Mechanism of action
Nefopam act on the brain to relive pain through inhibition of the reuptake of serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine, it also reduce glutamate signaling
It has no antipyretic or anti inflammatory activity
Therapeutic uses
It is used to treat moderate to severe pain
it is more potent analgesic than aspirin
Compared to morphine, 20mg of nefopam gives about same analgesia as 10 mg of morphine and there is no risk of respiratory depression in nefopam
Nefopam is also used to combat severe hiccups
It is used for prevention of shivering during surgery or recovery from surgery
Sweating, dizziness and nausea especially at higher doses
Precipitation of seizures in epilepsy patients (thus it is contraindicated)
Urinary retention
Tachycardia (aggravate angina)
Contraindications
Convulsive disorders
It is also contraindicated in patients who are being treated with monoamine oxidase inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressant because there is a risk for serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis
Overdose manifest as convulsions, hallucinations, tachycardia and hypertension
Nefopam overdose may lead to death
Treatment is supportive by limiting drug absorption by activated charcoal and managing the tachycardia (with beta blockers)

title: Acetaminophen Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Classification of analgesics
Opioid analgesics
Analgesics antipyretics drugs: e.g. acetaminophen, dipyrone and nefopam
Non analgesic drugs that work as analgesics for some conditions: e.g. carbamazepine (antiepileptic drug) used for trigeminal neuralgia, duloxetine (antidepressant) used for diabetic neuropathy
Scientific name is acetaminophen, trade names are paracetamol, Tylenol, Panadol …
Non opioid analgesic antipyretic that is used to treat fever and mild to moderate pain, it is the most commonly used medication for pain and fever in US, Europe
It was synthesized in 1878 by the American chemist Northrop Morse
Pharmacokinetics
Acetaminophen available oral, IV and rectal
Absorption of oral formula is rapid but the drug is extensively metabolized by first pass effect and bioavailability is dose dependent (50% at 500mg and 90% at 1000mg)

Metabolized by the liver via conjugation, a portion of the acetaminophen dose given will be hydroxylated to form N acetyl p benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI), which will react with sulfhydryl groups and cause liver damage
At normal doses of acetaminophen NAPQI will react with sulfhydryl group in glutathione (produced by liver) forming non toxic substance
At high doses, glutathione stores will be depleted, and NAPQI cause liver injury
Excretion is mainly renal
Mechanism of action
It inhibit prostaglandin synthesis in the brain which lead to the analgesic antipyretic effects of acetaminophen
It doesn’t inhibit prostaglandin synthesis in peripheral tissues because of peripheral inactivation, that is why it has weak anti inflammatory activity
Acetaminophen doesn’t affect PLT function unlike aspirin
It has little to no effects on CVS, GIT, respiratory or PLT function
Therapeutic uses
It is used as analgesic (for mild to moderate pain like headache, myalgia, mild MSK pain… ) and antipyretic
Paracetamol in arthritis pain is not effective and if it is given, it has to be combined with ibuprofen
It is useful in patients who can’t take NSAIDs because of gastric problems or they doesn’t need the extra anti inflammatory effects that comes with the NSAIDs
It is very safe in pregnancy (much better than aspirin)
It is used as analgesic/antipyretic in children with viral infections or chickenpox (due to risk of Reye syndrome with aspirin)
Paracetamol is inferior to NSAIDs in pain relief but it is safer and better tolerated by patients
Acetaminophen is well tolerated by most people
It may lead to allergic reactions (e.g. skin rash and fever)
Liver damage: In toxic doses of acetaminophen (about 15 g in adults, 4 g in children), there is hepatotoxicity (centrilobular necrosis) and it is sometimes associated with renal tubular necrosis
Acetaminophen overdose is the most common cause of acute liver failure

acetaminophen is metabolized by the liver via conjugation, a portion of the acetaminophen dose given will be hydroxylated to form N acetyl p benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI), which will react with sulfhydryl groups and cause liver damage
At normal doses of acetaminophen NAPQI will react with sulfhydryl group in glutathione (produced by liver) forming non toxic substance
At high doses, glutathione stores will be depleted, and NAPQI cause liver injury
Early symptoms of hepatic damage include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain, late symptoms include jaundice, edema… (liver failure)
Patients with hepatic disease are at higher risk of hepatic damage from acetaminophen
acetaminophen also lead to renal damage, hemolytic anemia, methemoglobinemia but those are rare
Treatment of acetaminophen overdose
Sulfhydryl donors (N acetyl cysteine) to restore hepatic glutathione. It is most effective if started within 8 hours of the drug administration
Hemodialysis: better within first 12 hours after ingestion
Acetaminophen Dosing
Dose of 325-500 mg four times daily, for children it is 10-15 mg/kg
Dosing in adults should not exceed 4g/d
Acetaminophen dose of 4g associated with LFTs abnormalities, so don’t exceed that dose

title: Naloxone Pharmacology: Treatment of Opioid Overdose, Mechanism of Action & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Naloxone is a synthetic opioid antagonist medication
It is famous for being used to counter the respiratory depression that occur with opioid overdose thus it is life saving medication
It was synthesized in 1961 by Mozes Lewenstein and Jack Fishman
Pharmacokinetics
Naloxone is mostly available as IV formula with a short duration of action (around 1-2 hours), it is also available IM, sub cut and intranasal
Oral formula not used because of extensive first pass metabolism (bioavailability is 2%)
Bioavailability of intranasal formula is 50% and the IV, IM are 100%
Metabolized by conjugation
Half life is from 30-80 minutes
Mechanism of action

Binds to the opioid receptors (mu, delta, kappa) and act as a competitive antagonist on these receptors and it has 10 times higher the affinity for mu opioid receptors, and that is why it is very good in reversing respiratory depression associated with the morphine and other opioid agonists
Administration of naloxone in patient not taking opioids would not produce any effect
In opioid dependent patients, antagonists rapidly reverse the effect of agonists (e.g. the effect of morphine) leading to withdrawal syndrome (explained in adverse effects chapter of this video)
Therapeutic uses
Opioid overdose: given IV to full agonist opioids overdose (e.g. morphine)

respiratory depression, level of consciousness, awareness of pain, cardiac arrest and other effects of opioid overdose are reversed within 1-2 min after IV naloxone administration and lasts for 1-2 hours duration

Patients who treated with naloxone IV may go back to respiratory depression after the duration of action of naloxone is over, so it has to be administered multiple times until the drug that caused overdose duration end
Treatment of opioid overdose
Naloxone is given with a dose of 0.1-0.4 mg IV for life threatening respiratory and CNS depression
Maintenance is with the same drug. Dose: 0.4-0.8 mg repeated whenever is necessary
In opioid overdose of the newborn, start with a naloxone dose of 5-10 mcg/kg and second dose of about the same amount if needed
Naloxone should be prescribed to patients taking high dose of opioids (> 100mg morphine) just in case they go into respiratory depression

And there should be a form of education that includes preventing, identifying and responding to opioid overdose, family members should be taught to give rescue breathing until emergency service reaches them
Therapeutic uses
Low dose naloxone 0.04 mg used in treatment of adverse effects associated with IV or epidural opioids
Naloxone also used in treatment of clonidine overdose (antihypertensive med)
It is given during labor to mothers who received opioids to prevent neonatal respiratory depression or it can be given to the neonate via the umbilical cord

Naloxone also combined with buprenorphine and pentazocine to prevent recreational opioid use of these medications because it is poorly absorbed orally (and that is why it is given orally so only buprenorphine or pentazocine are absorbed) and if the patient tries to IV administer the mix, naloxone would be absorbed there
There is no tolerance, no physical dependence and no addiction to opioid antagonists

Withdrawal syndrome is a number of symptoms that arise after sudden withdrawal or dose reduction of opioids that are consumed by an opioid physically dependent person, administration of naloxone equals opioid withdrawal but it is more severe because it occur in minutes
Withdrawal symptoms present as drug craving, anxiety, restlessness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, hyperventilation, muscle aches, tachycardia and hostility
Administration of naloxone may lead to hypotension, pulmonary edema and arrhythmias in patients with heart disease (please monitor for those)

title: Tramadol Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Tramadol is a synthetic opioid analgesic medication
Synthesized in 1963 in Germany and used commercially in 1977 under trade name Tramal
It is famous for producing less euphoria compared to other opioids, thus it is less addictive
Pharmacokinetics
Available as oral formulas (onset of pain relief after one hour of ingestion), also available as IV, IM and rectal formulas
Well absorbed with 70% oral bioavailability and 77% rectal

It undergoes extensive metabolism via CYP2D6 in the liver leading to desmethyltramadol which has more affinity to mu receptors and thus it is more active and lead to most of tramadol analgesic effects, some people has different variations of this enzyme that convert tramadol into inactive metabolites with no analgesic action
Excreted through the kidney
Tramadol Elimination half life is about 9 hours
Mechanism of action

Tramadol Bind to opioid receptors, especially mu receptors but it has low affinity to these receptors, it undergoes extensive metabolism via CYP2D6 leading to active metabolite which has much higher affinity for mu receptors which lead to its analgesic effects
It also block the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, so it increase their levels and may lead to serotonin syndrome (this is opposite to morphine, because morphine decreases norepinephrine)
Pharmacologic Effects
Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several central effects (CNS effects):
Analgesia: tramadol has one tenth the analgesic potency of morphine, means that tramadol has equal potency with pethidine and codeine, tramadol analgesia last for 6 hours
Euphoria: less euphoria than other opioids
Respiratory depression: less than morphine
Cough suppression
Nausea and vomiting
Pruritus due to histamine release
Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several peripheral effects including:
CVS: bradycardia and hypotension
GIT: constipation
Urinary system: may lead to urine retention
Immune: decrease immunity
Therapeutic uses
Used in treatment of moderate to severe pain – analgesic effect last for 6 hours
Used as a second line in treatment of fibromyalgia (first line being either pregabalin or duloxetine)
Also used in treatment of refractory restless legs syndrome (other opioids also effective in treatment of this condition)
Nausea and vomiting
Headache, drowsiness
Respiratory depression
Tolerance, physical dependence
Numbness, tingling, paresthesia, tinnitus due to increased serotonin and norepinephrine
Psychiatric symptoms: hallucinations, paranoia, anxiety, confusion due to increased serotonin
It may induce seizures in epileptic patients (relative contraindication)
Administration of naloxone can only partially reverse tramadol toxicity
Tramadol interact with other medications that increase serotonin levels (e.g. SSRIs) and may lead to serotonin syndrome
Contraindications
Pregnancy and lactation: due to neonatal withdrawal syndrome
Children under 12 and elderly due to high risk of respiratory depression
Liver and kidney failure due to accumulation
